Your Training

    selfmastery.mn.co/posts/self-mastery-course-ii-your-training-6431193




Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Image of Perfection lesson audio. You may want to listen more
than once.

2. Write about your judgments and scrutinize them. Write out the Judgement
statement. Hunt for the expectation of “What you should have done”. This is the standard,
expectation, or criteria of the judge. Write it out in detail.

3. Scrutinize that criteria of the Judge uses as “Perfection” How reasonable is
that criteria. Would you apply that standard to others? Would you say this judgment out
loud to others? How does the image of perfection the judge carries sound when you say it
out loud? If this is not socially acceptable, then that is a flag that the judgment has some
distortions to it.



Some notes

“What would it take for you to appease the voice of the Judge? “What criteria would you
have to meet for the Judge to say, “wow, you did great.” The more detailed you write up
this image of perfection the more ridiculous it is likely to become. The more ridiculous
this standard looks will help dissolve your faith in it faster.

That standard is what you are looking for. My suggestion is that you do this for one small
judgment on one issue at a time. Distill down to details. From the example of Bill’s story
about not being good enough you will see that I dug down to the details. This is extremely
helpful.

In this article you see the general list for one of my clients. In some ways it is detailed
enough, and in some places it lacks detail.Image of Perfection article.



Do NOT make a full list like this. This can be overwhelming and you might fall into the
viewpoint of the victim and believe the judge depending on where your emotions go. The
assignment is to do one at a time.





                                                                                                               1/2

Later, after you have good skepticism on the individual judgments, then you can compile
a list and see that stacked up together they contradict each other and find other flaws.
That can be good if you can stay outside and see that it is ridiculous. However, if you are
inclined to believe the judge, then a list like this, if believed, might invoke a “victim-not
good enough” response.

So make your list of criteria in a manner that you can see it as ridiculous and not get
overwhelmed.





                                                                                                               2/2

Obstacles you are likely to find

    selfmastery.mn.co/posts/self-mastery-course-ii-obstacles-you-are-likely-to-find-6431194

Goals are good. Goals are what we look towards, value, and steer our actions in the
direction of those goals. When we don’t have goals, or values we don’t know what to do, or
have motivation to do it.

When I ask you to dismantle the image of perfection, your judge will complain that “we
won’t have any goals, and so we will have no motivation, and so we will become a bum,
sleep all day, be lazy, and watch tv on the couch.” It will say you need those goals to keep
going.

Notice that I’m not asking you to question your goals. Image of perfection is different
than goals. Goals are things you go after in real life. Image of Perfection is the conceptual
idea your judge uses to put you down. That you could do without.

Differentiate between the goals you have for your life to focus on and work towards, and
the Image of Perfection that the Judge criticizes you for not having achieved yet. You may
find that some are the same.

Goal – I want to have a million dollars saved/invested for my retirement.

Then the judge says things like “you are such a failure. Other people have that but you just
aren’t good enough. You should’t have done XX in the past. That was really stupid.” This
is a demotivating narrative about an image of perfection not achieved, and how you failed
because the expected completion date was 10 years ago.

Other sources of motivation

The judge has been a big motivator, particularly for successful people. Their “prove I’m
worthy” strategy has driven them. If that is the case, they have come to rely on it for
motivation. It appears that the judge is the only source of motivation, if you have been
relying on it.

For the characters and the judge that live in the virtual world of the mind, this could
appear true to them. But, is that the only source of motivation for other people? What
other motivation do people have?

Maybe motivation can come from inspiration, love of what they do, appreciation of
quality, feeling of satisfaction for accomplishing something. Maybe motivation can be just
the desire to have a better life. If you don’t want to live under a bridge, and you want to
live in some place nice that is motivation. The reality of that motivation is at least real,
and better than what the judge does.

Motivation can come from other sources for other people, so it can come from other
sources for you too.




                                                                                                               1/2

So, if the judge is afraid that you will be without motivation, you have an answer. No. you
don’t have to be.

Then, you might notice that the judge is still afraid. However, if you dig further into the
cause of his fear, it might be that he is afraid of being without a job. If the judge no longer
has a job to do, he might feel like he will disappear. You might find that the judge is really
afraid of ceasing to exist.

If you feel that fear of dying, then this is progress.





                                                                                                               2/2

title: Module 21-Image of Perfection-21- SM - Image of Perfection - 03 Common Questions
method: Text extracted from the original written course handout.

Common Questions

   selfmastery.mn.co/posts/self-mastery-course-ii-common-questions-6431195

What if the criteria of the judge appears true when I look at it?


Are you looking with the eyes of the victim (tendency to believe the judge) or are you
looking as a skeptic.

Notice your emotions. If you are in the emotions of the victim, then you are likely in that
point of view.



What if you want to keep the image of perfection as a goal?

It’s your life and your world. You are free to do whatever you wish. My suggestion is
always do it with awareness. What characters might be involved in keeping the image of
perfection? What emotions do you feel about not yet having achieved that goal? Are you
past a deadline that the judge has a criticism about?

Are they in alignment with your happiness? Do they believe that achieving the goal
(different body, money, partner, material things) will change your emotions? Is this really
true?

Many times we are attached to those things because we are attached to the emotions we
have connected to those things.

Keep the goals, but practice breaking the judges pattern of using them as a club on you
emotionally.

What constitutes your image of perfection? Take the judgmental thoughts you have and
look at the criteria of expectation that is behind the judgment. In other words, what
criteria do you have to attain in order for the Inner Judge to finally say, “Congratulations,
you made it.” These hidden beliefs result in thoughts of being a failure and create
emotions of unworthiness. By having an image of perfection in our mind we give credence
to the voice in our head that puts us down. If we bring these dynamics into our awareness
we have the opportunity to change them and rid ourselves of not feeling good enough.

My battle with the Image of Perfection Beliefs

came up with the following list. It is a core belief inventory of what she is supposed to be.
She was in Graduate School at the time and sent me two sections, one about being a
woman, and the other about being a scholar. As you read notice how these criteria
contradict each other. With conflicting criteria in our subconscious it becomes impossible
